question: Which Annex lays down the SARPs for establishing air traffic services in each State?

options.text: Annex 6
Annex 11
Annex 15, together with aeronautical information
Annex 2

explanation: Annex 11 contains the SARPs for air traffic services; each State designates an authority responsible for setting up and regulating its ATS.

question: Which document gives the detailed procedures for air traffic management, complementing Annex 11?

options.text: Doc 9432, the radiotelephony manual used by controllers
Doc 7030 (Regional Supplementary Procedures)
Doc 4444 (PANS-ATM)
Doc 8168 (PANS-OPS)

explanation: Annex 11 SARPs are not detailed enough, so PANS-ATM (Doc 4444) is the reference for establishing and managing an ATS; crews should know its parts on ATM, separation, ADS/CPDLC, incident reports and RPLs.

question: Which of these is an objective of air traffic services?

options.text: To provide weather forecasts for the flight
To approve operators' flight plans for economy
To investigate accidents and serious incidents and publish the final reports
To notify organizations about aircraft needing search and rescue aid

explanation: The ATS objectives are to prevent collisions between aircraft and with obstructions on the manoeuvring area, expedite and maintain an orderly flow, provide useful advice and information, and notify SAR organizations.

question: Air traffic services comprise:

options.text: Air traffic control service, flight information service and alerting service
Area control, approach control and aerodrome control only
Flight information, meteorological, aeronautical information and search and rescue services
Air traffic control and search and rescue

explanation: ATS has three divisions: air traffic control service, flight information service and alerting service.

question: The air traffic control service is divided into:

options.text: En-route control and ground movement control only
Flight information, alerting, advisory and aeronautical information services
Radar and procedural control only
Area control, approach control and aerodrome control services

explanation: ATC service is sub-divided into area control, approach control and aerodrome control services.

question: Approach control service is the ATC service for:

options.text: All traffic on the manoeuvring area
VFR traffic in an aerodrome traffic zone only
Controlled flights arriving or departing
Controlled flights in control areas en route

explanation: Area control serves controlled flights in control areas; approach control serves arriving and departing controlled flights; aerodrome control serves aerodrome traffic.

question: Which factor is considered when deciding whether air traffic services are needed?

options.text: The cost of the service to the State
The density of traffic
The nationality of the aircraft using the airspace
The number of airlines based at the aerodrome

explanation: The need for ATS considers the types of traffic, traffic density, meteorological conditions and other factors such as terrain, sea areas and navaids.

question: When deciding the level of air traffic service needed in an area, how is the carriage of ACAS by aircraft taken into account?

options.text: It is not taken into account
It counts as one of the main factors in the decision
It allows ATC to be replaced by flight information service
It allows a lower level of service

explanation: The carriage of ACAS by aircraft in an area shall not be a factor in determining the need for air traffic services.

question: Air traffic control service is provided to:

options.text: All flights in a flight information region
All flights that have filed a flight plan, whatever the airspace
Controlled flights, and aerodrome traffic at controlled aerodromes
IFR flights in all airspace classes

explanation: ATC is provided to controlled flights inside controlled airspace or to aerodrome traffic at controlled aerodromes.

question: In which airspace classes do VFR flights receive air traffic control service?

options.text: A, B and C
C, D and E
B, C, D and E
B, C and D

explanation: ATC is always provided to IFR flights in controlled airspace but only to VFR flights in classes B, C and D; all special VFR flights receive ATC.

question: ATS units comprise:

options.text: Approach units and meteorological offices
Air traffic control units and flight information centres
Towers and rescue coordination centres
Area control centres only

explanation: ATS units are ATC units (providing ATC) and flight information centres (providing FIS); the FIS and alerting service may be provided by the same unit.

question: Can one approach control unit provide approach control for several aerodromes?

options.text: Yes, as a combined approach control unit
No, each aerodrome must have its own approach unit
Only for military aerodromes
Only if the aerodromes share a single runway

explanation: Combined approach control offices exist where approach control for several aerodromes or CTRs is provided from one unit.

question: At a large aerodrome, the movement of aircraft and vehicles on the apron may be delegated to:

options.text: An apron management service
The area control centre
The approach controller
The aircraft operators, who coordinate among themselves

explanation: Ground movement is the aerodrome controller's responsibility, may be delegated to a ground movement controller, and on the apron to an apron management service.

question: Which time reference do ATS units use?

options.text: Local time, using the 24-hour clock
Local time for VFR flights and UTC for IFR flights
UTC, using the 12-hour clock
UTC, using the 24-hour clock

explanation: ATS units use co-ordinated universal time (UTC), in hours, minutes and (where required) seconds of the 24-hour day.

question: ATS unit clocks must be accurate to within:

options.text: ±15 seconds of UTC
±5 seconds of UTC
±30 seconds of UTC
±1 minute of UTC

explanation: ATSU clocks and timing devices are checked to ensure they are within ±30 seconds of UTC at all times; time checks are rounded to the nearest minute.

question: An ATC clearance is defined as:

options.text: Permission to enter a flight information region
Authorization to proceed under conditions specified by an ATC unit
An instruction that the pilot must follow even if unsafe
Information about known traffic given by an ATS unit to help the pilot avoid collisions

explanation: A clearance is authorization to proceed under conditions specified by an ATC unit.

question: On what basis are ATC clearances issued?

options.text: To ensure terrain clearance for the aircraft
Solely to expedite and separate traffic, based on known traffic conditions
To give the most economical route
To ensure that every aircraft avoids significant weather and terrain along its route

explanation: Clearances are issued solely for expediting and separating air traffic, based on known traffic conditions, including traffic moving on the ground.

question: A pilot requests an alternative to an unsuitable clearance. What should the pilot understand?

options.text: It will be given if possible, but may cause delay
The flight must return to the departure aerodrome
It must always be given immediately
The original clearance is cancelled and the flight must hold

explanation: An alternative clearance may be requested and offered if possible, but alternative clearances may result in delays.

question: When should an ATC clearance be issued?

options.text: Only when the aircraft requests it on the frequency
At least 30 minutes before departure
Early enough to allow sufficient time to comply with it
Only after the aircraft has entered controlled airspace

explanation: A clearance must be issued early enough for there to be sufficient time to comply with it.

question: When flying in accordance with an ATC clearance, the pilot is:

options.text: Relieved of responsibility for terrain clearance
Relieved of the rules of the air
Relieved of all responsibility until the clearance limit
Still responsible for safety, including terrain avoidance

explanation: A clearance does not relieve the pilot of responsibility for the safety of the aircraft (including terrain avoidance) or of the rules of the air.

question: Who ensures obstacle clearance when an aircraft is being radar vectored?

options.text: The operator, by publishing safe headings in its manual
Nobody, as vectors are given only above the MSA
The radar controller, through the clearances issued
The pilot alone, as during any other phase

explanation: Under radar vectoring, the radar controller issues clearances such that the required obstacle clearance exists at all times.

question: In controlled airspace, which flights are always separated from each other?

options.text: VFR flights from other VFR flights
IFR flights from VFR flights in all classes
Special VFR flights from VFR flights
IFR flights from other IFR flights

explanation: Within controlled airspace IFR is always separated from IFR; in classes B and C IFR is also separated from VFR, and in class B VFR from VFR. SVFR flights are normally separated in a CTR.

question: Which item is included in an ATC clearance?

options.text: The clearance limit
The fuel on board
The number of passengers on board
The weather at the alternate

explanation: A clearance includes the aircraft identification, clearance limit, route, level(s), and other necessary instructions or information such as SIDs, STARs, communications or clearance expiry time.

question: When is the transition level included in an approach clearance?

options.text: Only for aircraft without an FMS
When prescribed, or when requested by the pilot
Always
Never; it is only given by ATIS

explanation: The transition level is included in approach clearances if so prescribed or when requested by the pilot.

question: In which clearance is the QNH included (unless the aircraft is known to have it)?

options.text: In the clearance to climb above the transition altitude
When first cleared to an altitude below the transition level
In the en-route clearance at the cruising level
In the start-up clearance only

explanation: QNH is included when first cleared below the transition level, in approach clearances, in circuit-entry clearances and in taxi clearances for departing aircraft.

question: Which ATC unit is responsible for issuing the route clearance for a flight?

options.text: The ACC of the FIR where the flight originates
The ACC of the destination FIR
The tower at the destination aerodrome
The ACC of the FIR where the flight spends the longest time

explanation: The ACC of the FIR where the flight originates issues the route clearance, ideally coordinated with the other ACCs en route.

question: A clearance cannot be coordinated for the whole route of a long flight. What happens?

options.text: The flight must fly VFR outside the first FIR
The flight is refused departure
The flight must land at each FIR boundary
It is cleared progressively, FIR by FIR (downstream clearances)

explanation: Clearances are then given on a rolling (downstream) basis; the aircraft may be asked to obtain a downstream clearance itself before entering the next FIR.

question: Which instruction must always be read back?

options.text: Traffic information
A request to report the runway in sight
A clearance to cross a runway
A wind check on final approach

explanation: Read-back is required for route clearances and for clearances to enter, land on, take off from, hold short of, cross or backtrack on any runway, among others.

question: Which of these must be read back by the pilot?

options.text: A frequency to monitor ATIS
The ATIS weather
A request to say level
An SSR code

explanation: Read-back is required for runway in use, altimeter settings, SSR codes, level, heading and speed instructions, and transition levels.

question: What is the main practical advantage of air traffic flow management (ATFM)?

options.text: Aircraft always fly the shortest route
Predictable delays are absorbed on the ground before take-off
Aircraft hold at the destination rather than en route
All flights are given equal priority in the air, so holding is shared fairly between them

explanation: ATFM predicts overloads and delays take-off so delays are taken on the ground rather than in the air, with economic, environmental and safety benefits.

question: Who controls the movement of persons and vehicles, including towed aircraft, on the manoeuvring area?

options.text: The apron management service
The airport police
The aerodrome control tower
The airline ground handling agent

explanation: The movement of persons or vehicles, including towed aircraft, on the manoeuvring area is controlled by the aerodrome control tower as necessary to avoid hazards.

question: During low visibility procedures, persons and vehicles on the manoeuvring area are:

options.text: Kept to a minimum
Unrestricted if they hold radio
Escorted by a follow-me car
Allowed only on the apron

explanation: When low visibility procedures are in force, persons and vehicles operating on the manoeuvring area are restricted to the essential minimum.

question: What special measure is taken during CAT II/III operations regarding vehicles and aircraft on the ground?

options.text: Only towed aircraft may cross the runway
ILS/MLS sensitive areas are protected
All vehicles must use hazard lights
Taxiing is suspended at night

explanation: Special procedures safeguard the ILS/MLS critical and sensitive areas when CAT II/III operations are in progress.

question: Emergency vehicles going to an accident on the aerodrome:

options.text: Must give way to taxiing aircraft
Must wait for a tower clearance at each crossing
Have priority only over other vehicles, and must still give way to all aircraft
Have priority over all other surface movement traffic

explanation: Emergency vehicles proceeding to assist an aircraft in distress are given priority over all other surface movement traffic.

question: Vehicles on the manoeuvring area must give way to:

options.text: Other vehicles only
Only aircraft taking off
Aircraft landing, taking off or taxiing
Pedestrians only

explanation: Vehicles and vehicles towing aircraft give way to aircraft landing, taxiing or taking off.

question: A vehicle meets a vehicle towing an aircraft on the manoeuvring area. Which gives way?

options.text: The vehicle not towing an aircraft
The slower of the two vehicles
The vehicle on the left
The vehicle towing the aircraft

explanation: Vehicles give way to vehicles towing aircraft; other vehicle priorities follow ATS unit instructions.

question: Whatever the general right-of-way rules, vehicles on the manoeuvring area must:

options.text: Use only the marked service roads and never enter a runway at any time
Comply with instructions from the aerodrome control tower
Follow the instructions of the airline staff
Always give way to other vehicles

explanation: Notwithstanding the other rules, vehicles and vehicles towing aircraft comply with instructions issued by the aerodrome control tower.

question: Flight information service relies heavily on which service?

options.text: The search and rescue service
The air traffic flow management unit
The aerodrome rescue and fire fighting service
The aeronautical information service

explanation: FIS relies on a regular flow of information, especially from the AIS established under Annex 15. Inside controlled airspace FIS is provided at lower priority than ATC.

question: A unit giving flight information service uses which call sign suffix?

options.text: "Control"
"Radar"
"Information"
"Approach"

explanation: A unit providing FIS is suffixed "Information" (e.g. "London Information"); FIS officers may not provide any service that could be described as ATC.

question: To which aircraft is flight information service provided?

options.text: Aircraft likely to be affected, if receiving ATC or otherwise known to ATS
Only IFR aircraft
Only aircraft that request it before take-off and file a full flight plan with the unit
Only aircraft in uncontrolled airspace

explanation: FIS is provided to all aircraft likely to be affected by the information which are provided with ATC or are otherwise known to the ATS units.

question: Which item is included in flight information service?

options.text: Passenger connection times at the destination
Information on unmanned free balloons
Fuel prices at aerodromes
Airline schedules

explanation: FIS includes SIGMET and AIRMET, volcanic activity, release of radioactive or toxic materials, changes in navaid serviceability, aerodrome conditions and unmanned free balloons.

question: Flight information service also includes information on collision hazards to aircraft operating in which airspace classes?

options.text: C, D, E, F and G
A and B only
F and G only
All classes, including class A

explanation: FIS includes weather at departure, destination and alternates, collision hazards in classes C to G, and, on request over the sea, information on surface vessels.

question: AIRMET information concerns en-route weather phenomena which may affect:

options.text: All aircraft at all levels, including jets cruising in the upper airspace above FL300
Only supersonic aircraft
Only aircraft above FL250
Low-level operations, and is not already in the low-level forecast

explanation: AIRMET is information on specified en-route phenomena that may affect low-level operations and were not already included in the forecast for low-level flights.

question: SIGMET information is issued by:

options.text: The operator's dispatch office
The aerodrome control tower
A meteorological watch office
The area control centre

explanation: SIGMET is issued by a meteorological watch office about specified en-route phenomena that may affect the safety of aircraft operations.

question: VOLMET broadcasts contain:

options.text: Traffic information for VFR flights and position reports from other aircraft in the area
METAR, TAF and SIGMET for groups of aerodromes, on a schedule
Only NOTAM for the FIR
Departure clearances for IFR flights

explanation: VOLMET (HF and VHF) broadcasts METAR, TAF and SIGMET for specific aerodromes or groups, according to a schedule.

question: Who is responsible for preparing and disseminating ATIS?

options.text: The meteorological office
The national AIS office
Air traffic services
The aerodrome operator

explanation: ATIS comprises voice ATIS and data link ATIS (D-ATIS); its preparation and dissemination is the responsibility of ATS.

question: Which arrangement of voice ATIS broadcasts is permitted?

options.text: Separate arrival and departure broadcasts, if one would be too long
One broadcast per runway in use, each updated every hour on the hour by the tower
A single broadcast for all aerodromes in the FIR
Separate broadcasts for each airline

explanation: Voice ATIS may be one broadcast for arrivals, one for departures, one for both, or two (arrivals and departures) where one would be exceptionally long.

question: On which frequency is voice ATIS never transmitted?

options.text: A frequency published on the aerodrome chart
A discrete VHF frequency
The voice channel of a VOR
The voice channel of an ILS

explanation: Voice ATIS is transmitted on a discrete VHF frequency or the voice channel of a relevant VOR, but never on the voice channel of an ILS.

question: An ATIS broadcast should normally not last longer than:

options.text: 2 minutes
15 seconds
1 minute
30 seconds

explanation: An ATIS message should not exceed 30 seconds; it is updated immediately on a significant change and identified by a sequential letter.

question: On first contact with ATC, how should a pilot show that the current ATIS has been received?

options.text: By stating the time it was heard
By quoting the QNH only
By quoting the ATIS designator letter
By reading back the whole ATIS to the controller on first contact

explanation: Aircraft acknowledge receipt of the relevant ATIS by referring to its current designator letter.

question: An ATIS broadcast includes cloud information when the cloud base is below:

options.text: 1500 ft in all cases
5000 ft or the highest MSA (whichever is higher), or with CB
3000 ft or the lowest MSA (whichever is lower), or when towering cumulus is reported
10 000 ft or the transition level

explanation: Cloud cover is included only when the base is below 1500 m (5000 ft) or the highest MSA, whichever is higher, or when cumulonimbus is present.

question: A pilot acknowledges an ATIS that is no longer current. What will ATC do?

options.text: Transmit the elements that need updating without delay
Refuse the clearance until the new ATIS is quoted
Nothing; the pilot is responsible
Read the whole new ATIS to the pilot and ask for a full read-back of it

explanation: If an aircraft acknowledges an ATIS that is no longer current, any element needing updating is transmitted to the aircraft without delay.

question: Which ATS units provide the alerting service?

options.text: Only area control centres
Only rescue coordination centres and the units that they appoint
Only aerodrome control towers
Any ATS unit, whatever service it normally provides

explanation: The alerting service is provided by any ATS unit; where necessary it has priority over all other air traffic services.

question: To which aircraft is the alerting service provided?

options.text: Only aircraft that have declared an emergency by radio or by squawking 7700 on the transponder
Aircraft under ATC, others known to ATS where practicable, and hijacked aircraft
Only IFR flights
Only aircraft flying over the sea

explanation: Alerting service goes to all aircraft provided with ATC, as far as practicable to others with a flight plan or otherwise known, and to aircraft known or believed to be subject to unlawful interference.

question: Which ATS units serve as the central point for collecting emergency information and passing it to the rescue coordination centre?

options.text: Approach control units
Apron management units at the departure and destination aerodromes
Flight information centres and area control centres
Aerodrome control towers

explanation: FICs and ACCs collect all information on an aircraft's emergency and forward it to the appropriate RCC.

question: An emergency arises while an aircraft is under aerodrome control. What does the tower do?

options.text: Notify the ACC or FIC; alert local services itself if urgent
Contact the rescue coordination centre only
Ask the aircraft to contact the area control centre itself
Wait until the aircraft has landed

explanation: The aerodrome or approach unit notifies the ACC or FIC, which notifies the RCC; if the situation is urgent, it sets local emergency services in motion itself.

question: An aircraft is subject to unlawful interference. How does ATC refer to this on the radio?

options.text: It makes no reference unless the aircraft has mentioned it first
It uses the code word "hijack" in all messages
It announces it to all aircraft on the frequency
It asks the crew to confirm the details immediately so that other traffic can be warned

explanation: No reference is made in ATC communications unless it has first been mentioned by the aircraft and it will not make the situation worse.

question: The uncertainty phase (INCERFA) exists when:

options.text: The aircraft is known to be subject to unlawful interference
The aircraft fails to land within 5 minutes of the estimated landing time and cannot be contacted
Fuel is considered to be exhausted
No contact for 30 minutes after it was due, or 30 minutes overdue at destination

explanation: INCERFA: no communication within 30 minutes after it should have been received, or failure to arrive within 30 minutes of the ETA.

question: An aircraft cleared to land fails to land within 5 minutes of the estimated landing time and communication cannot be re-established. Which phase is declared?

options.text: Distress phase (DETRESFA)
No phase; the tower waits 30 minutes
Alert phase (ALERFA)
Uncertainty phase (INCERFA)

explanation: The alert phase is declared if the aircraft fails to land within 5 minutes after the landing clearance, if attempts at communication fail, if operating efficiency is impaired, or if it is subject to unlawful interference.

question: Information is received that an aircraft's operating efficiency is impaired so that a forced landing is likely. Which phase applies?

options.text: Alert phase, then distress after 30 minutes
Distress phase (DETRESFA)
Alert phase (ALERFA)
Uncertainty phase (INCERFA)

explanation: DETRESFA applies when enquiries indicate distress, fuel is considered exhausted, efficiency is impaired so a forced landing is likely, or a forced landing is about to happen or has happened.

question: When ATC uses speed control, which practice applies?

options.text: Give adequate notice and avoid prolonged use
Ask for speeds in multiples of 5 kt
Change speed frequently to keep separation tight
Use it only above FL250

explanation: Speed control may be used to maintain separation; adequate notice is given, prolonged use is not recommended, and changes are limited to those needed.

question: At or above FL250, speed adjustments by ATC are expressed in multiples of:

options.text: 10 kt IAS
20 kt IAS
Mach 0.01
Mach 0.05

explanation: At or above FL250 adjustments are in multiples of Mach 0.01; below FL250, in multiples of 10 kt IAS.

question: On intermediate and final approach, ATC speed adjustments should not exceed:

options.text: ±10 kt
±30 kt
±40 kt
±20 kt

explanation: On intermediate and final approach, speed changes are limited to minor adjustments of not more than ±20 kt IAS.

question: After what point on final approach should speed control not be applied?

options.text: 2 NM from the threshold
4 NM from the threshold
10 NM from the threshold
The final approach fix

explanation: Speed control is not applied to aircraft after passing a point 4 NM from the threshold of the landing runway.

question: ADS-B is a system in which aircraft:

options.text: Receive their position from ground stations
Reply to interrogations from ground radar
Report their position by voice to ATC every 10 minutes on a dedicated frequency
Broadcast their position, identity and velocity

explanation: In ADS-B the aircraft continuously broadcasts position, altitude, category, speed, identification and vertical trend over a data link; range is line of sight.

question: Basic ADS reports consist of latitude, longitude, altitude, time and:

options.text: Wind at the aircraft's position
A figure of merit (accuracy)
Number of persons on board
Fuel remaining

explanation: Basic ADS consists of latitude, longitude, altitude, time and figure of merit.

question: A routine air-report (AIREP) has three sections. Which section is always mandatory?

options.text: Section 1 — position report
Sections 2 and 3 together
Section 2 — operational information
Section 3 — meteorological information

explanation: Section 1 (position) is mandatory; Section 2 (ETA and endurance) is sent when requested or considered necessary; Section 3 (met) when the aircraft has been asked to make routine met reports.

question: Which phenomenon must be reported in an AIREP SPECIAL?

options.text: Light rain at cruising level
Moderate turbulence
Severe icing
A temperature 5°C warmer than forecast

explanation: AIREP SPECIAL is required for severe turbulence, severe icing, severe mountain wave, obscured/embedded/widespread or line-squall thunderstorms, heavy dust or sandstorms, and volcanic ash.

question: A pilot experiences an AIRPROX. How is the report initially made?

options.text: By the controller only; the pilot has no role
In writing within 7 days only
By the operator after reviewing the flight data
By radio, and then completed on the ground

explanation: Air traffic incident reports include AIRPROX, procedure and equipment reports; a pilot files the initial AIRPROX report by RTF and completes it on the ground.

question: An aircraft is believed to be subject to unlawful interference. How is it treated by ATC?

options.text: It is ordered to land at the nearest aerodrome
It is given no special treatment unless it declares MAYDAY
It is given priority over other aircraft
It is handled after all other traffic

explanation: An aircraft known or believed to be in a state of emergency, including unlawful interference, is given priority over other aircraft.

question: Two aircraft with similar call signs are on the same frequency. What may ATC do?

options.text: Use only the registration of both aircraft
Instruct one aircraft to change its call sign temporarily
Require both aircraft to use their flight plan numbers in reverse order
Ask one aircraft to leave the frequency

explanation: ATC may require an aircraft to change its call sign temporarily when there is a risk of confusion with a similar call sign on the same frequency.
